lesson.menu_title: The Ninety-Day Question — What You Would Recommend to the Board
lesson.menu_desc: Turning the first ninety days into three formal recommendations a board can endorse, in order -- 33 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 18 -- The Ninety-Day Question
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Fernando Meneghelli Bottura | Lesson 18 -- The Ninety-Day Question

listenings.text: I chair the board of a media group, and I have interviewed six finance directors in the last ten years. The question I always ask is what they would bring to the board after ninety days. The weak answer is that they would listen. Of course they would listen. The strong answer gives me three things. One problem they expect to find, one quick win they could deliver in the first quarter, and one thing they would deliberately not do yet. The last one is the rarest. A candidate who tells me he would put off a project he likes is a candidate who understands that a board has limited attention, and limited cash.

When I was a young finance director, my board papers were full of soft language. Perhaps we could consider looking at the costs. My chair sent one of them back to me with a single note in the margin: recommend something. So I learned to write it differently. I recommend that the board approve a hiring freeze in the central functions until June. It is essential that the savings be used for the technology project and nothing else. Nobody in that room thought I was being arrogant. They thought I had done the work. A recommendation is a decision you are asking somebody else to take, and it should sound like one.

extra_audio.text: Claire asks what he would bring to the board after ninety days. He recommends a quick win: a five-day close. She asks whether that is realistic, and he insists that every unit head sign off their own figures. He suggests that the board ring-fence the technology budget and defer the new office. He says the third recommendation depends on what he finds.

reading.rtitle: What chairs listen for in the ninety-day answer
paras: Ask a CFO candidate what he would do in his first ninety days, and most will give the same answer: listen, learn and meet the team. The chairs interviewed for this note said that answer is not wrong, but it is not a recommendation. What they want to hear is what the candidate would put forward to the board, and in what order.

The strongest candidates separate the quick wins from the roadmap. A quick win is something the board will notice in the first quarter: a faster monthly close, a weekly cash report, a supplier contract that nobody has renegotiated in years. The roadmap is what takes a year, and it is where candidates lose credibility, because they promise everything at once. One chair said she trusts the candidate who recommends that the company phase in the big changes and defer at least one project he would personally like to start.

The language matters too. A recommendation that sounds like a wish, such as maybe we could look at the costs, gives the board nothing to endorse. A recommendation that is formal and specific does: I recommend that the board ring-fence the technology budget, and it is essential that the forecast be reviewed by the business units before it comes back here. Directors said the formal structure tells them the candidate has written board papers before.
None of this means arriving with all the answers. The candidates who impress chairs say clearly which recommendations depend on what they find, and which ones they would make on any first day.
reading.source: Adapted from board practice notes on CFO appointments

gist.prompt: What is the main point of this text?
choices: Chairs want a CFO candidate to promise every change in the first ninety days, from the monthly close to the whole technology roadmap.
Chairs listen for specific, formal recommendations in a clear order, not a plan to listen and learn.
Chairs prefer candidates who arrive with all the answers.
